characters.name: Susan Rodriguez

characters.description: Knight of the Cross and Harry's steadfast friend, bearer of the sword Amoracchius. Michael and his fellow Knights come to Chicago on the trail of the stolen Shroud of Turin and the monsters hunting it, and he once again stands between Harry and the worst of what follows. His faith, his family, and his patience with Harry's recklessness are all tested by an enemy older and crueler than any they have faced together.
characters.name: Michael Carpenter

characters.description: The eldest of the three Knights of the Cross: a small, elderly Japanese man of unassuming warmth who carries Fidelacchius, a holy blade hidden in a cane. A onetime blues-loving convert with a lifetime of battles behind him, Shiro is deceptively gentle in manner and devastating in a fight. He takes a particular, quiet interest in Harry, and his choices in this case leave a mark on Harry that lasts for years.
characters.name: Shiro Yoshimo

characters.description: The youngest Knight of the Cross: a towering, cheerful Russian who wields the sword Esperacchius and, despite his office, professes to be an agnostic - he fights for what the swords do, not for certainty about who sends them. A former Denarian host who was freed and chose the other side, Sanya brings good humor, an assault rifle's pragmatism, and firsthand knowledge of the enemy.
characters.name: Sanya

characters.description: The leader of the Order of the Blackened Denarius: fallen angels bound into ancient silver coins, each granting its human host monstrous power in exchange for the demon's growing control. Nicodemus has held his coin for two thousand years and remains fully himself - which makes him worse than any of his possessed followers, a genial, cultured man who plans in centuries and kills without hesitation. He wears an ancient noose at his throat, comes to Chicago for the Shroud of Turin, and takes a connoisseur's interest in breaking Harry Dresden.
characters.name: Nicodemus Archleone

characters.description: The Archive: the living repository of all human knowledge ever written, an office passed down a single bloodline - currently vested, unsettlingly, in a solemn little girl. Bound to perfect neutrality, she serves as emissary and arbiter for the duel between Harry and Ortega. Harry, unable to treat her as an institution, calls her Ivy, and the small kindness registers. Her composure conceals power on a scale that gives even wizards pause.
characters.name: The Archive

characters.description: The Archive's bodyguard and driver: a laconic, lethally competent mercenary who handles supernatural threats with mortal weapons and total professionalism. Kincaid is friendly enough off the clock and utterly without sentiment on it, and there are persistent hints that he is something more than human. He and Harry develop a wary mutual respect over the course of the duel arrangements.
characters.name: Kincaid

characters.description: Chicago's crime lord, who inserts himself into the hunt for the stolen Shroud with his usual cold efficiency. Marcone's interest in the relic is intense, personal, and unexplained, and as ever he is willing to cooperate with Harry exactly as far as it serves his own ends. His performance under fire in this case shows again why he rules the city's underworld.
characters.name: John Marcone

characters.description: A professional thief, one of a three-person crew called the Churchmice who stole the Shroud of Turin from Turin's cathedral. Cool-headed and skilled, Anna Valmont finds the score of a lifetime turning into a death sentence as buyers and monsters converge on the relic, and her surviving the sale becomes entangled with Harry's job of recovering it.
characters.name: Anna Valmont

recaps.ending: Harry recovers the Shroud of Turin and stops Nicodemus from unleashing the plague curse he had bound to it, holding the Denarian off in a fight aboard his escaping train - Nicodemus, nearly unkillable, is driven off rather than destroyed, and remains at large. The victory is bought with Shiro's life: the old Knight traded himself to Nicodemus for Harry's freedom, endured torture without breaking, and dies of it, leaving his sword Fidelacchius in Harry's keeping until its next bearer appears. The duel with Ortega ends in treachery - Ortega breaks the terms when he loses, the duel collapses into open violence, and he fails to kill Harry; the war goes on. Susan, whose control and new strength with the Fellowship of St. Giles carried Harry through the worst of the fight, leaves Chicago again for the Fellowship's war, and she and Harry part as lovers who cannot have a life together. Marcone ends the affair in possession of the Shroud, his reasons still his own. In the final scene, at the Carpenter home, one of the Denarians' coins - Lasciel's, planted deliberately - rolls toward Michael's youngest son, and Harry slaps his bare hand over it to save the boy. He buries the coin under his lab, but the touch was enough: the fallen angel's shadow now lives in his mind, a secret he tells no one.
recaps.in_short: Harry is hired to recover the stolen Shroud of Turin just as the Red Court warlord Ortega arrives to challenge him to a formal duel to end the vampire war. Susan returns, half-turned but trained by the Fellowship of St. Giles; the three Knights of the Cross - Michael, the old swordsman Shiro, and the cheerful Russian Sanya - arrive hunting the Order of the Blackened Denarius, fallen angels in silver coins led by the two-thousand-year-old Nicodemus, who wants the Shroud to power a plague curse. Nicodemus captures and nearly kills Harry; Shiro trades himself for Harry's life and dies under torture. The duel with Ortega ends when the losing vampire breaks its terms, and the war continues. Harry stops the plague and reclaims the Shroud - which ends up in Marcone's hands - while Susan leaves again for the Fellowship's fight. At the last, to keep a planted coin from Michael's young son, Harry covers it with his bare hand and takes the shadow of the fallen angel Lasciel into his own mind - and tells no one.

recaps.text: Previously: Harry Dresden, Chicago's professional wizard, ignited a war between the wizards' White Council and the Red Court of vampires when he burned the vampire Bianca's court to save Susan Rodriguez - his girlfriend, who was left half-turned by the Red Court's bite and fled the city rather than risk the people she loves. The Council kept Harry under its protection after he cleared the Winter Queen Mab of murdering the Summer Knight, a case that ended with the Summer Lady Aurora dead and Harry owing Mab two more tasks. Detective Karrin Murphy now knows the whole truth of his world; Michael Carpenter, a Knight of the Cross, is his most trusted ally; and the war with the Red Court grinds on, with Harry a marked man.

Two jobs land on Harry at once. A priest, Father Vincent, hires him to recover the Shroud of Turin, stolen from its cathedral by a crew of professional thieves called the Churchmice. And Paolo Ortega, a courtly warlord of the Red Court, arrives with a formal challenge under the Accords: a duel to the death with Harry, offered as a way to end the war between the vampires and the White Council - if Harry dies, the Council is spared; if he refuses, the war consumes everyone around him. Harry accepts. Susan Rodriguez returns to Chicago after more than a year away, changed - stronger, faster, and in control of her half-vampire thirst, thanks to the Fellowship of St. Giles, an order of the half-turned who war against the Red Court. And bodies begin turning up around the stolen Shroud, killed in ways that point to something far worse than thieves.

The Knights of the Cross converge on Chicago: Michael, the elderly Japanese swordsman Shiro, and Sanya, a towering Russian who used to carry one of the enemy's coins. Their quarry is the Order of the Blackened Denarius - fallen angels bound in ancient silver coins, each riding and consuming a mortal host - led by Nicodemus Archleone, who has kept his own will through two thousand years with his coin and wants the Shroud for a purpose of his own. The Denarians butcher their way through the Churchmice; the thief Anna Valmont survives, and Harry's attempt to intercept the Shroud's sale goes violently wrong. Marcone, too, is maneuvering for the relic, his reasons unexplained. The Knights warn Harry to stay out of the Denarians' path; Harry, being Harry, does not.

Nicodemus captures Harry, entertains him with urbane menace at his own table, and, when Harry refuses a place in his order, has him bled and left to die - and Harry learns the Denarians' plan: the Shroud will anchor a plague curse designed to kill on a massive scale. Shiro trades himself to Nicodemus in exchange for Harry's freedom, knowing exactly what will be done to him. Battered and running out of time, Harry still has the duel to fight: with the Archive - a solemn little girl who is the living record of all written knowledge - as arbiter and her mercenary Kincaid keeping order, Harry meets Ortega in a duel of wills. Harry wins, and spares him; Ortega answers by breaking the duel's terms, and the formal contest collapses into open bloodshed from which both sides pull back wounded. The war is not over, and the plague is still coming.

Harry, Michael, Sanya and Susan run the Denarians down before the plague curse can be unleashed. Shiro, tortured past what any man should bear, is recovered dying; he passes his sword Fidelacchius to Harry, to hold in trust for the bearer who will come for it, and dies. In the final fight aboard Nicodemus's escaping train, Harry seizes the ancient noose the Denarian wears - one of the few things that can harm him - reclaims the Shroud, and breaks the curse; Nicodemus survives and escapes, minus his prize. The Shroud finishes the affair in Marcone's possession. Susan leaves Chicago again for the Fellowship's war against the Red Court, and she and Harry part still in love and still impossible. Then, at the Carpenter home, a silver coin - planted in a farewell trap - rolls toward Michael's youngest son. Harry covers it with his bare hand before the boy can touch it. He buries the coin beneath his lab, but the contact has already done its work: the shadow of the fallen angel Lasciel has taken up residence in his mind, and Harry tells no one.

characters.description: An aging traveling salesman who returns unexpectedly to his Brooklyn home after becoming too exhausted and distracted to drive safely. He measures success through popularity, personal charm, and material proof, yet his career is failing and his memories increasingly interrupt the present. He places his greatest hopes in his elder son, Biff.
characters.name: Willy Loman

characters.description: Willy's devoted wife, who manages their dwindling finances and protects his dignity while seeing his decline more clearly than their sons do. She knows that he has been borrowing money and fears that his car crashes and a hidden rubber hose indicate repeated attempts to end his life.
characters.name: Linda Loman

characters.description: Willy and Linda's elder son, now thirty-four, who has drifted among outdoor jobs in the West since leaving school. Once a celebrated high-school athlete, he feels both affection and deep anger toward his father. He returns home uncertain whether to accept the business future Willy imagines or acknowledge that it has never suited him.
characters.name: Biff Loman

characters.description: The Lomans' younger son, employed in business and living in his own apartment. Outwardly confident and socially successful, he privately admits to loneliness and pursues women with little regard for commitments. He shares Willy's faith in appearances and eagerly joins Biff's plan for a sporting-goods venture.
characters.name: Happy Loman

characters.description: Willy's neighbor and long-time friend, a plainspoken businessman who plays cards with him and quietly lends him money each week. Charley offers practical help without demanding admiration, which makes Willy both dependent on him and resentful of his success.
characters.name: Charley

characters.description: Charley's son, remembered as a studious boy who tried to help Biff pass mathematics. As an adult he has become a successful lawyer preparing to argue a case before the Supreme Court, though he remains modest and treats Willy kindly.
characters.name: Bernard

characters.description: Willy's adventurous elder brother, seen mainly in memories and imagined conversations. He left home young and emerged rich from distant ventures, becoming Willy's symbol of decisive risk and spectacular success. Willy repeatedly seeks his approval when reality becomes difficult.
characters.name: Ben Loman

characters.description: A woman in Boston with whom Willy has an affair during his years on the road. In Willy's memories she laughs with him, flatters his importance, and receives stockings from him, while his guilt about the relationship intrudes upon his life with Linda.
characters.name: The Woman

characters.description: The young head of the company Willy has served for decades and the son of Willy's former employer. Preoccupied with his family and a new wire recorder, he listens to Willy's request for work close to home but evaluates him by his present sales rather than past loyalty.
characters.name: Howard Wagner

characters.description: A waiter at the restaurant where Biff and Happy arrange to meet Willy. He knows Happy and serves the family during an evening that deteriorates as Biff tries to explain the failure of his business meeting.
characters.name: Stanley

characters.description: A young woman Happy approaches at the restaurant while waiting for Willy. Happy falsely presents himself and Biff as important businessmen and invites her to join them.
characters.name: Miss Forsythe

recaps.ending: After Biff finally states that neither he nor Willy is destined for exceptional business success, he breaks down and weeps in his father's arms. Willy recognizes Biff's love but misunderstands the confrontation as proof that Biff can still fulfill his ambitions. Convinced that the insurance payment from his death will give Biff the capital and status he lacks, Willy drives away and deliberately crashes his car. Only Linda, Biff, Happy, Charley, and Bernard attend the funeral. Biff concludes that Willy pursued a mistaken dream and intends to return to the outdoor life that suits him. Happy rejects that judgment and vows to prove that Willy's vision of success was right. Charley defends the hopes on which a salesman depends. Linda, unable to understand why Willy died just after the last house payment was made, addresses him at the grave. The family is free of the mortgage but divided over the meaning of Willy's life and death.
recaps.in_short: Exhausted salesman Willy Loman returns to his Brooklyn home as his career and grasp on the present fail. He clings to memories of his sons' promising youth and believes Biff can still become a business success. Biff, now a restless adult, agrees to seek financing, but the meeting fails; on the same day Willy is fired. At dinner Biff tries to tell the truth, while Willy retreats into the memory of Biff discovering his affair in Boston, the event that destroyed the boy's trust and ambitions. Back home Biff rejects the family's inflated dreams and insists that both men accept their ordinary selves. Willy sees Biff's tears as renewed faith in him and kills himself in a car crash so Biff can receive the insurance money. The funeral is sparsely attended. Biff abandons Willy's dream, while Happy vows to continue it, and Linda mourns beside a house whose mortgage has finally been paid.

recaps.text: Sixty-three-year-old salesman Willy Loman returns to his Brooklyn home after abandoning a trip because he could no longer drive safely. His wife Linda urges him to ask his employer for local work. Their adult sons, Biff and Happy, are visiting. Biff has spent years drifting among outdoor jobs and feels unable to meet Willy's expectations; Happy has a business job but is dissatisfied. Willy slips between the present and memories of the boys' adolescence, when he celebrated Biff's athletic popularity and dismissed warnings about study and theft. His successful brother Ben appears in these recollections as the model of wealth Willy never achieved. Neighbor Charley lends Willy money that Willy pretends is salary, though Willy rejects Charley's offer of a job. Linda tells the sons that their father's crashes may be deliberate and that she found a rubber hose suggesting another suicide plan. Ashamed, Biff agrees to ask former employer Bill Oliver to finance a sporting-goods business with Happy. The plan and a temporary reconciliation restore Willy's hope.

Willy asks Howard Wagner for a non-traveling position, but Howard dismisses his claims of past service and fires him. Willy then meets the now-successful Bernard, who asks why Biff abandoned his future after visiting Willy in Boston. Willy avoids the answer. Charley again offers him a job and gives him money, but Willy's pride lets him accept only the loan. At a restaurant Biff tries to explain that Bill Oliver barely remembered him and never considered him a salesman; after waiting all day, Biff impulsively stole Oliver's fountain pen. Willy refuses this correction to the family's story and announces that he has been fired. As the conversation collapses, Happy leaves with two women and denies that Willy is his father. Willy relives Boston, where teenage Biff discovered him with another woman. Biff's admiration broke, and he abandoned the summer school needed for graduation. At home Linda condemns both sons for deserting Willy. Biff confronts his father, rejects their fantasies of greatness, and says he will leave. His tears convince Willy that Biff loves him. Believing his life-insurance money will make Biff successful, Willy consults the imagined Ben and drives away to kill himself.

Willy dies in the planned car crash. Despite his belief that personal popularity would bring a great public farewell, only Linda, Biff, Happy, Charley, and Bernard gather at his grave. Charley argues that a salesman's work depends on dreams and that Willy was destroyed when those dreams ceased to sustain him. Biff believes Willy misunderstood himself and spent his life pursuing the wrong kind of success; he plans to leave the business world and return to work outdoors. Happy instead vows to remain in the city and demonstrate that Willy's ambition was valid. Linda cannot reconcile the suicide with the family's new financial position: the mortgage has just been paid, and she had imagined that they were finally secure. She says goodbye at the grave, left with an empty, fully owned house. Willy's death ends his struggle but passes the conflict over his values to his sons.

characters.description: Now in his forties: the pagan warlord on whom Christian Wessex has depended for thirty years, holder of an estate in Mercia and of a tangle of oaths - to the dying Alfred, and above all to Alfred's daughter Aethelflaed, his lover and lady. Bebbanburg, his stolen birthright in the north, remains unclaimed. As Alfred's death approaches and every ambitious man in Britain sharpens a knife, Uhtred is the sword both sides want and neither trusts.
characters.name: Uhtred

characters.description: King of Wessex for a generation and the architect of the dream of a single Christian England, now plainly dying. Reduced in body but not in will, he spends his final strength arranging the succession of his son Edward and binding the kingdom's dangerous men - Uhtred first among them - to survive him. Whatever lies between him and Uhtred, three decades of war have made them each other's habit.
characters.name: Alfred

characters.description: Alfred's son and designated heir: earnest, unproven, and raised in his father's piety, about to inherit a kingdom that many powerful men believe should not be his. The Danes expect to carve up England on Alfred's death, and Edward's ability to hold Wessex - and to use hard instruments like Uhtred - is the great open question of the succession.
characters.name: Edward

characters.description: Alfred's nephew, son of the king who reigned before him, who has spent a lifetime nursing the conviction that the throne of Wessex was stolen from him. Weak, drunken, and endlessly plausible, he has plotted with Danes before and been forgiven too often. With Alfred dying, his claim finally becomes useful to powerful men - which makes him, at last, truly dangerous.
characters.name: Aethelwold

characters.description: Alfred's daughter, lady of Mercia in everything but title: braver and more loved than her husband Aethelred, and Uhtred's lover, bound to him by an oath freely given. As her father dies and her brother inherits, she is the hinge holding Wessex and Mercia together against the Danish storm.
characters.name: Aethelflaed

characters.description: A great Danish jarl of the north midlands, rich in ships and men, who sees Alfred's coming death as the moment to destroy Wessex forever. Harder-headed than the raiders of earlier wars, he works by scheme as well as sword - buying prophecies, laying traps, and gathering the Danish lords toward one great war for England.
characters.name: Sigurd

characters.description: Sigurd's closest ally, a pale, quick Danish jarl reputed the deadliest swordsman in Britain. Soft-spoken and amused where Sigurd is blunt, he is the more frightening of the pair for it. Together they command the strength of the Danish north and wait for the death of a king to loose it.
characters.name: Cnut

characters.description: An aged sorceress living at a pagan shrine, famed across Britain: men travel far to hear her prophecies, and Danes and Saxons alike fear her. Her visions of dead kings and Danish victory run ahead of the coming war - but a prophecy can be bought, and whoever pays the prophet shapes what the credulous will believe.
characters.name: Aelfadell

characters.description: The Irish warrior who has stood at Uhtred's shoulder since their shared slavery at the oar: his second in command, his sharpest blade, and his most trusted friend through every campaign of the last twenty years.
characters.name: Finan

characters.description: Alfred's bastard son, long since traded the monastery for the shield wall as one of Uhtred's household warriors. Careful, devout, and quietly formidable, he serves the man his father never fully trusted while his half-brother prepares to inherit the crown - a position he bears with his usual patience.
characters.name: Osferth

recaps.ending: The book ends with the great Danish bid for England defeated in a bleak winter battle. Three years after Alfred's death, the Danes invade in strength, with Aethelwold riding among them as their claimant to the West Saxon throne and King Eohric of East Anglia joined to their cause. The armies meet in a grinding shield-wall battle in which the Danish coalition is broken apart rather than cleanly beaten: Eohric is killed, several Danish leaders fall, Sigurd is wounded, and Uhtred himself kills Aethelwold, ending forever the rival claim that had shadowed Edward's succession. The surviving Danes, unable to keep the field through the winter, withdraw. The title's promise is kept several times over - Alfred dead in his bed, Eohric and the pretender Aethelwold dead in battle - and Edward sits securely as king of Wessex, his father's dream of one England battered but alive. Uhtred, prophesied by the sorceress Aelfadell to be the doom of kings, has been exactly that, though not in the way the Danes who paid for the prophecy hoped. He remains what he was: Aethelflaed's sworn man and lover, the pagan shield of the Christian kingdoms, with Bebbanburg still waiting unclaimed in the north.
recaps.in_short: As the book opens in 899, Alfred is dying and every ambitious man in Britain is waiting. A peace overture from East Anglia proves a trap laid by the jarl Sigurd, which Uhtred fights his way out of; the famed sorceress Aelfadell, whose prophecies foretell Danish victory and the death of kings, turns out to be paid by Sigurd to say so, and Uhtred counters her by staging three women as Christian angels spreading rival prophecy. Alfred dies, rewarding Uhtred and binding him toward his heir; Edward is crowned, and Alfred's embittered nephew Aethelwold - convinced the throne is rightfully his - flees to the Danes, giving Sigurd and Cnut the royal figurehead their invasion needs. Three years later the Danish coalition strikes. In a brutal winter battle the invasion is broken: King Eohric of East Anglia is killed, Sigurd is wounded, and Uhtred personally kills Aethelwold, extinguishing the rival claim. The Danes withdraw, and Edward is secure on his father's throne, with Uhtred still Aethelflaed's sworn man and still dreaming of Bebbanburg.

recaps.text: Previously: Uhtred of Bebbanburg - Saxon-born, raised by Danes, dispossessed of his northern fortress by his uncle - has spent thirty years as the sword of Christian Wessex without ever loving it: he killed Ubba, helped Alfred save the kingdom at Ethandun, avenged his Danish foster father by taking Dunholm alongside his foster brother Ragnar, and won and lost two loves, the shadow queen Iseult and his Danish wife Gisela, who died in childbirth. In The Burning Land he crushed Harald Bloodhair at Fearnhamme, then broke with Alfred's court after killing a cleric who insulted Gisela's memory, fled north to Ragnar, and plotted to invade Wessex at the head of a Danish army - until Aethelflaed, Alfred's daughter and the holder of his oath, called him back. He became her sworn man and her lover, led Mercia's forces, and stormed the Danish stronghold at Beamfleot, breaking the power of the treacherous jarl Haesten, who escaped as he always does. Now Alfred is dying at last; his earnest son Edward waits to inherit, his resentful nephew Aethelwold covets the throne, and the Danish lords of the north - Sigurd Thorrson and Cnut Ranulfson chief among them - gather for the war they believe will finally destroy Wessex.

Through the end of Part One (The Sorceress): the book opens in 899 with Alfred visibly dying and all Britain waiting on his death. Uhtred, lord of a modest Mercian estate and still Aethelflaed's sworn man, is drawn into the manoeuvring at once: a supposed peace overture involving King Eohric of East Anglia proves to be a trap laid by the Danish jarl Sigurd, and Uhtred fights his way clear of an ambush meant to remove Wessex's best warrior before the real war begins. Rumour of prophecy runs ahead of the armies - the aged sorceress Aelfadell, famed across the island, foretells the death of kings and the triumph of the Danes, and her visions unsettle Saxon and Dane alike. Uhtred travels into the Danish north to hear her for himself and pays for his curiosity: drugged and held at her shrine, in the country of the jarl Cnut Ranulfson, he learns the truth that the prophetess's visions are bought and paid for by Sigurd - propaganda dressed as fate, aimed at breaking Saxon confidence before a spear is thrown. He escapes with the knowledge, and with the prophecy that he himself will be the doom of kings hanging over him.

Through the end of Part Two (Death of a King): Alfred's long dying reaches its end. The old king spends his final strength settling his legacy - rewarding Uhtred and working to bind the pagan warlord he never trusted to the cause of his son and heir - and then Alfred, king of Wessex for a generation and architect of the dream of one Christian England, dies. Edward is crowned king of Wessex: earnest, untested, and surrounded by men measuring him against his father, he inherits a kingdom that every Danish lord in Britain believes is now ripe to fall. The succession is immediately contested from within - Aethelwold, Alfred's nephew, who has spent thirty years nursing the conviction that the throne was stolen from him when his own father died, refuses to accept Edward's crown, and his long-tolerated scheming finally turns to open treachery. War is now a certainty; only its timing and its shape remain in question, and Uhtred - bound to Aethelflaed, and through her to her brother's cause - stands as the shield of a new, unproven king.

Through the end of Part Three (Angels): Aethelwold flees to the Danes, offering Sigurd and Cnut the thing their invasion has always lacked - a royal Saxon claimant to legitimize conquest - and the Danish lords proclaim him the rightful king of Wessex. Uhtred fights prophecy with prophecy: to counter Aelfadell's bought visions of Danish triumph, he stages three women posing as Christian angels whose rival foretellings steady Saxon nerves and sow doubt among the credulous on both sides. Around these moves the two camps gather their strength - Edward consolidating his father's kingdom and feeling his way into his crown, the Danish lords assembling the great coalition of the north, with East Anglia's King Eohric drawn toward their cause - while Uhtred holds the Mercian frontier with Finan, Osferth, and his household troops, and Aethelflaed anchors Mercia against the storm everyone knows is coming.

Through the end of Part Four (Death in Winter) - the book's close: three years after Alfred's death, the Danish coalition finally strikes, invading in strength with Aethelwold riding among them as their claimant to the West Saxon throne and King Eohric of East Anglia joined to their cause. The campaign ends in a grinding winter shield-wall battle in which the coalition is broken apart rather than cleanly beaten: Eohric is killed, several Danish leaders fall with him, Sigurd is wounded, and Uhtred himself cuts down Aethelwold, ending forever the rival claim that had shadowed Edward's succession. The surviving Danes, unable to keep the field through the winter, withdraw. The title is paid in full - Alfred dead in his bed, Eohric and the pretender Aethelwold dead in battle - and Edward sits securely as king of Wessex, his father's dream of one England battered but alive. Aelfadell's prophecy that Uhtred would be the doom of kings has come true, though not as the Danes who paid for it hoped. Uhtred ends the book as he began it: Aethelflaed's sworn man and lover, the pagan shield of the Christian kingdoms, with Bebbanburg still unclaimed in the north.

characters.description: A young Englishwoman who has inherited an American fortune and is admired everywhere she goes for her looks, her money and her competence. She buys a country estate, reorganises it, and is used to arranging the world to suit herself, including the lives of the people who depend on her. She is generous by habit and does not always notice what her generosity costs other people.
characters.name: Linnet Ridgeway

characters.description: Linnet's school friend, small, dark, and intense, whose family lost everything and who now has nothing at all. She is passionately in love with Simon Doyle and says so without embarrassment. She comes to Linnet to ask a favour for him, and warns, half laughing, that she loves too fiercely for her own good.
characters.name: Jacqueline de Bellefort

characters.description: A large, good-looking, cheerful young man with no money and no head for office work, engaged to Jacqueline de Bellefort. He is straightforward to the point of simplicity, hates towns, and wants a job in the country where he can manage land.
characters.name: Simon Doyle

characters.description: The Belgian detective, on holiday and determined to remain on holiday, who keeps meeting the principals of this affair by accident, first in a London restaurant and then in Egypt. He gives warnings that nobody takes and observes people at length in the sun.
characters.name: Hercule Poirot

characters.description: A pleasant, sensible Englishwoman of limited means travelling with her son, on whom she dotes and about whom she is not deceived. She makes friends easily and enjoys Poirot's company.
characters.name: Mrs Allerton

characters.description: Mrs Allerton's son, an idle, charming young man of uncertain health and uncertain occupation, who lives abroad cheaply and writes a book he never finishes. He is a distant cousin of Linnet's circle and is vague about his London acquaintances.
characters.name: Tim Allerton

characters.description: An American trustee of the Ridgeway fortune, one of the firm that has managed Linnet's money since her father died. Hearty and expansive in manner, he turns up in Egypt claiming a chance meeting and is anxious to have documents signed without too much reading.
characters.name: Andrew Pennington

characters.description: A British colonel with a vague official position, travelling on the Nile steamer in pursuit of an agitator believed to be aboard under an assumed identity. Dry, capable and discreet, he has worked with Poirot before and shares the investigation with him.
characters.name: Colonel Race

characters.description: A once-popular novelist of overheated romances, now drinking heavily and convinced that her books are suppressed by conspiracies. She talks loudly about her work to anyone within reach and is a constant embarrassment to her daughter.
characters.name: Salome Otterbourne

characters.description: Salome Otterbourne's daughter, a sullen, defensive young woman worn out by managing her mother and hiding the bottles. Her rudeness is armour, and Poirot treats it as such.
characters.name: Rosalie Otterbourne

characters.description: An elderly and immensely snobbish American, travelling with a companion and a nurse and interested only in people whose families she recognises. She is rude to nearly everyone and expects deference as a matter of course.
characters.name: Miss Van Schuyler

characters.description: Miss Van Schuyler's poor relation and unpaid companion, a plain, patient young American who is fetched and scolded all day and considers herself lucky to be travelling at all. She is kinder and shrewder than anybody gives her credit for.
characters.name: Cornelia Robson

characters.description: A calm, sturdy hospital nurse engaged to attend Miss Van Schuyler, professionally incurious and entirely unimpressed by her employer's rank. She keeps her patient's business to herself.
characters.name: Miss Bowers

characters.description: A stout, elderly Austrian physician of considerable European reputation, travelling for pleasure and pleased to lecture anyone who will listen. His cabin becomes the ship's sickroom when it is needed.
characters.name: Dr Bessner

characters.description: A scruffy, loudly opinionated young man who denounces wealth, leisure and the whole class of people travelling with him, and is particularly offensive about Linnet Doyle. He takes an interest in Cornelia Robson and is contemptuous of Miss Van Schuyler.
characters.name: Mr Ferguson

characters.description: Linnet Doyle's French maid, who dresses her, guards her jewellery and is discontented with her position and her prospects of marriage. She is quick to feel a slight and quick to see an advantage.
characters.name: Louise Bourget

recaps.ending: Poirot and Race establish that Simon Doyle and Jacqueline de Bellefort planned everything together. Their public quarrel, the broken engagement and the relentless pursuit across Europe and Egypt were staged so that each would have an unassailable alibi. In the saloon Jacqueline fired a shot that hit nothing; as soon as the witnesses had scattered to fetch help, Simon picked up the pistol, went to his wife's cabin, shot her through the head, returned, scrawled a letter J on the wall to incriminate Jacqueline, and then shot himself through the leg to produce the wound he had been carried away with. Jacqueline retrieved and disposed of the pistol wrapped in a stolen velvet stole. She afterwards killed the maid Louise Bourget, who had tried to blackmail them, and shot Mrs Otterbourne through the door as she was about to name the person she had seen. The purpose was Linnet's fortune, after which Simon would in time have married Jacqueline. Confronted, Simon breaks down. As they are being taken off the steamer, Jacqueline uses a second small pistol to shoot Simon and then herself, sparing them both a trial. The other threads settle: Pennington's frauds are exposed, Miss Van Schuyler's thefts are managed quietly by her nurse, Tim Allerton returns the pearls he had replaced with a copy and is let off by Poirot on condition he goes straight, and Tim and Rosalie Otterbourne leave together, as do Cornelia Robson and Dr Bessner.
recaps.in_short: Linnet Ridgeway, a young and much-envied heiress, marries Simon Doyle, the penniless fiance of her friend Jacqueline de Bellefort, who had asked her to give him a job. Jacqueline follows the honeymoon couple across Europe and up the Nile, appearing wherever they go, until all three are aboard the steamer Karnak with Poirot and Colonel Race. After a boulder narrowly misses Linnet at a temple, Jacqueline drunkenly shoots Simon in the leg one night in the saloon and is taken away sedated. In the morning Linnet is found shot in her bed with the letter J written in blood on the wall. Two more deaths follow: the maid Louise Bourget, stabbed after hinting that she knew something, and Salome Otterbourne, shot as she is about to name a witness. Poirot shows that Simon and Jacqueline committed the murders together, the long public feud having been staged to give each of them an alibi, with Linnet's fortune as the object. Jacqueline shoots Simon and herself rather than face arrest.

recaps.text: Linnet Ridgeway, young, beautiful and enormously rich, buys a country estate and rearranges the neighbourhood to suit it. Her school friend Jacqueline de Bellefort, who has nothing, comes to ask a favour: that Linnet employ her fiance Simon Doyle, a big, cheerful, unemployable young man, as land agent. Linnet meets him and marries him herself. The scandal travels ahead of them. Poirot, dining in a London restaurant, watches Jacqueline and Simon together before the marriage and hears the intensity with which she speaks of him. Various other people are shown preparing to travel: Mrs Allerton and her idle son Tim, the American trustee Andrew Pennington in New York, a young man with violent opinions about the rich, and others whose paths will cross in Egypt. Linnet and Simon leave on honeymoon and find Jacqueline waiting for them at each stop, silent, smiling and always visible, which no law can prevent and which is slowly wearing them both down.

At Assuan the Doyles arrive at the hotel where Poirot is staying, and Jacqueline arrives with them. Linnet begs Poirot to make her stop; Poirot instead goes to Jacqueline and warns her that she is opening her heart to evil, and she shows him the small pearl-handled pistol she carries. Simon tries a blunter approach and gets nowhere. During an excursion to a temple a boulder crashes down from above and narrowly misses Linnet, though Jacqueline was demonstrably elsewhere. The party boards the steamer Karnak for the journey up the Nile, and Jacqueline books a passage at the last moment. The other passengers include Colonel Race, travelling on official business of his own, the novelist Salome Otterbourne and her daughter Rosalie, the imperious Miss Van Schuyler with her companion Cornelia Robson and her nurse Miss Bowers, the Austrian Dr Bessner, the aggressive young Mr Ferguson, Pennington the trustee, the Allertons, and Linnet's French maid Louise Bourget. Poirot watches the tension aboard tighten day by day.

One night in the observation saloon Jacqueline, who has been drinking, taunts Simon until she snatches out her pistol and fires at him, hitting him in the leg. Cornelia Robson and a young fellow passenger get her away to her cabin, where Miss Bowers sedates her and stays with her; Simon is carried to Dr Bessner's cabin and his leg set. In the confusion the pistol disappears from the saloon. In the morning Linnet is found shot through the head as she slept, with a letter J daubed in blood on the wall above her, and her string of pearls missing from the dressing table. Colonel Race joins Poirot in the investigation, since the steamer is beyond any police force and everyone aboard is a suspect. The medical evidence puts the death in the small hours, and both Jacqueline and Simon appear to have been watched over all night.

Poirot and Race work through the passengers. The pistol is dredged up from the river wrapped in a velvet stole belonging to Miss Van Schuyler, with two shots fired from it and the stole scorched and holed. The pearls turn up and prove to be a good imitation. Miss Bowers admits that she is employed to watch Miss Van Schuyler, whose habit of taking other people's property is a family affliction, and that the old lady took the pearls and returned them. Pennington's business papers show that he has been speculating with Linnet's fortune and needed her signature, and his story of a chance meeting collapses. Others have their own reasons for discomfort: Rosalie Otterbourne is protecting her mother's drinking, Ferguson conceals more than his politics, and Tim Allerton is evasive about his London connections. Louise Bourget, the maid, hints in front of witnesses that she may have seen something, refuses to say what, and is later found dead in her cabin, stabbed, with a torn corner of a banknote in her hand.

Salome Otterbourne comes to Poirot and Race announcing that she saw who went into the maid's cabin, and is shot dead through the doorway before she can give the name. The shot is fired with a pistol taken from Race's own cabin, and the passengers' movements at that moment are again nearly impossible to fix. The steamer turns back with three bodies aboard. Poirot resolves the lesser mysteries as he goes: the imitation pearls were substituted for the real ones by Tim Allerton, working with a London acquaintance who supplied the copies; the agitator Race has been hunting is aboard under an assumed archaeological identity; and Pennington's frauds, though real, do not fit the shape of the murders. Poirot returns to the physical facts of the first killing, in particular the stole used to muffle the shot, the two bullets, and the exact sequence of the evening in the saloon.

Poirot lays out the truth. Simon Doyle and Jacqueline de Bellefort acted together, and the whole public spectacle of the jilted girl pursuing the honeymoon couple was arranged to give each of them a perfect alibi. In the saloon Jacqueline fired a shot that hit nothing; the moment the witnesses had gone for help, Simon took the pistol, went to his wife's cabin, shot her, wrote the letter J on the wall, and then shot himself through the leg, so that the wound he was carried away with was self-inflicted and the timing was false. Jacqueline recovered the pistol and sank it in the river wrapped in the stolen stole. She afterwards stabbed Louise Bourget, who had seen enough to attempt blackmail, and shot Mrs Otterbourne through the door before she could identify her. The object was Linnet's fortune, which Simon would inherit as her husband, after which the two intended to marry in a decent interval. Simon breaks down when confronted with the evidence. As the pair are taken off the steamer, Jacqueline shoots Simon and then herself with a second small pistol she had kept. Pennington is left to answer for his frauds, Tim Allerton returns the pearls and is given a chance to reform, and he and Rosalie leave together, while Cornelia Robson accepts Dr Bessner.

characters.description: A quiet, unworldly Oxford theology student whose blameless routine is destroyed when drunken members of a club strip off his trousers. The university expels him for indecency, and financial necessity sends him into schoolteaching under an assumed appearance of experience.
characters.name: Paul Pennyfeather

characters.description: The headmaster of Llanabba Castle, a poorly run private school in Wales. He recruits Paul with little scrutiny, manages crises through bluff and optimism, and treats the school's disorder as a normal condition of business.
characters.name: Dr. Fagan

characters.description: A fellow master at Llanabba with a military title, a wooden leg, and an extensive history of escaping failed careers and difficult marriages. Cheerfully adaptable, he regards almost every disaster as temporary.
characters.name: Captain Grimes

characters.description: A former clergyman teaching at Llanabba after losing his faith. Timid, melancholy, and chronically uncertain, he explains his troubles to Paul while trying to maintain order among boys who do not respect him.
characters.name: Mr. Prendergast

characters.description: Llanabba's enigmatic domestic servant, who offers different grand accounts of his past whenever the occasion demands. His confidence and apparent competence make the truth of his identity almost beside the point.
characters.name: Philbrick

characters.description: A self-possessed pupil at Llanabba and the son of the wealthy Margot Beste-Chetwynde. He quickly recognizes Paul's inexperience but treats him with friendly interest and introduces him to a more fashionable world.
characters.name: Peter Beste-Chetwynde

characters.description: Peter's wealthy, glamorous mother. Recently widowed and surrounded by fashionable associates, she takes an immediate interest in Paul when she visits Llanabba, whose social occasion improves markedly in her presence.
characters.name: Margot Beste-Chetwynde

characters.description: Dr. Fagan's daughter, who helps with the school and hopes to marry Captain Grimes. Her position requires her to treat Llanabba's recurring emergencies with a mixture of practicality and resignation.
characters.name: Flossie Fagan

characters.description: A fashionable architect employed to rebuild Margot's country house, King's Thursday. His severe modern design and abstract pronouncements give physical form to the novelty and rootlessness of Margot's circle.
characters.name: Otto Silenus

characters.description: A Black American guest in Margot's social circle and a subject of excited curiosity to people around him. He is treated less as an individual than as a vehicle for their assumptions about race, culture, and fashion.
characters.name: Chokey

characters.description: A senior politician whose position gives him influence over the machinery of law and punishment. His later connection with Margot makes that official power personally important to Paul's fate.
characters.name: Sir Humphrey Maltravers

recaps.ending: In prison Paul encounters distorted versions of his earlier life: Philbrick is an inmate, Prendergast has become a chaplain, and Grimes reappears before making another improbable escape. A prisoner kills Prendergast during a disturbance. Margot, whose business caused Paul's conviction, has protected herself by marrying the politically powerful Sir Humphrey Maltravers. She and her allies arrange for Paul to undergo an operation, be declared dead under another identity, and leave custody. Paul returns to Oxford disguised by a moustache and enters his old college as a supposed distant relative of the expelled Paul Pennyfeather. He resumes theological study with little outward change as the university and the club culture that caused his fall continue their familiar routines. Society has moved Paul through disgrace, employment, luxury, and punishment without ever establishing a meaningful connection between guilt and consequence.
recaps.in_short: Oxford student Paul Pennyfeather is expelled after drunken aristocrats steal his trousers, though he has done nothing wrong. Forced to teach at a chaotic Welsh school, he meets the resilient Captain Grimes, the doubtful Prendergast, and wealthy pupil Peter Beste-Chetwynde. Peter's glamorous mother Margot hires Paul as a tutor and becomes engaged to him. Paul remains incurious about her international entertainment business until he is arrested for assisting its traffic in women and accepts punishment rather than implicate her. In prison he meets former colleagues in new roles, while Margot protects herself by marrying an influential politician. Her circle arranges Paul's false death and release after an operation. He returns to Oxford under the identity of his own distant relation and resumes theology, while the institutions that arbitrarily expelled and punished him continue unchanged.

recaps.text: Paul Pennyfeather, an inoffensive Oxford theology student, is caught in the path of a drunken club whose members strip him of his trousers. College officials punish Paul for public indecency while the well-connected offenders face no meaningful consequence. Expelled and deprived of his inheritance income, he applies through an agency for work as a schoolmaster. He is sent to Llanabba Castle, a private school in Wales run by Dr. Fagan. Paul arrives with no teaching experience and joins a staff of social and professional failures, including the irrepressible Captain Grimes and the troubled former clergyman Mr. Prendergast. The school is short of resources, discipline, and academic purpose, but everyone proceeds as though this were ordinary.

Paul struggles to supervise boys who immediately detect his weakness, though pupil Peter Beste-Chetwynde treats him with friendly amusement. Llanabba prepares an elaborate sports day intended to impress parents. The event exposes the institution's incompetence: arrangements fail, guests are mismanaged, and a starting pistol causes a serious injury. Peter's mother Margot arrives and transforms the occasion through wealth and social confidence. She takes an interest in Paul. Captain Grimes, meanwhile, approaches his proposed marriage to Dr. Fagan's daughter Flossie as one more situation from which circumstances may eventually release him.

Paul leaves Llanabba to work for Margot as Peter's private tutor. At King's Thursday he enters a fashionable household being radically rebuilt by the modern architect Otto Silenus. Margot's associates accept novelty, money, and confident performance more readily than moral scrutiny. Paul falls in love with Margot, and their social difference creates surprisingly little obstacle. He hears references to her overseas entertainment enterprises without investigating what they require. His passivity, which helped him endure school life, now allows him to participate in arrangements whose nature he does not understand.

Margot and Paul become engaged. As the wedding approaches, Paul undertakes business errands for her involving the recruitment and transport of young women abroad. The work is presented to him in respectable administrative terms, and he does not press beyond them, although other people understand that Margot's organization supplies women to brothels. Authorities arrest Paul before the marriage can take place. Social influence insulates Margot while evidence and Paul's willingness to protect her concentrate responsibility on him. He is tried, convicted of trafficking, and sentenced to a long term of imprisonment.

Paul enters a prison system whose officials classify and reform him according to theories unrelated to his actual character. He adapts with the same mild acceptance he showed at school. Former figures from his life recur in altered positions: Philbrick is among the prisoners, Prendergast serves as a prison chaplain, and Captain Grimes again appears within confinement. A violent inmate kills Prendergast during disorder in the prison. Grimes escapes, continuing his pattern of surviving institutions and apparent disasters. Paul is transferred and increasingly becomes an object managed by administrators rather than a person whose innocence matters.

Margot avoids prosecution and marries Sir Humphrey Maltravers, whose political power allows her circle to intervene in Paul's case without publicly reversing it. Paul is sent for an operation and officially reported dead; the deception enables him to leave custody with a changed appearance. He returns to Oxford as a supposed relative of the disgraced Paul Pennyfeather and quietly resumes the theological studies from which he was expelled. Around him, the college and the drunken club continue their established routines. Paul's circular return closes a sequence in which institutions repeatedly assigned him the identities of offender, teacher, criminal, and reformed prisoner without showing any reliable concern for his actual conduct.
